newsitem.title: USA: Geron stock soars on cloning breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Geron stock soars on cloning breakthrough.

text.p: The stock of Geron Corp. more than doubled Friday after the biotech company revealed it has sucessfully cloned a gene that could potentially be used to fight cancer and aging-related diseases.
Geron soared $7.50 to close at $14 on Nasdaq, where it was the second most active issue. Earlier, the stock hit a high of $17.125.

Late Thursday, Menlo Park, Calif.-based Geron announced it had sucessfully cloned the gene for the human telomerase catalytic protein. Telomerase is an "immortalizing enzyme" that allows cancer cells to reproduce endlessly, unlike other normal human cells (except reproductive cells) that have finite life spans.

Geron hopes that it can develop a telomerase blocker that could be used to effectively treat cancer. Since telomerase is not present in normal cells, the treatment is hoped to have fewer side-effects than existing cancer therapies.
Under the same principal, telomerase could be used to combat aging-related diseases.
Geron's partner in the project is the University of Colorado, Boulder.

"The cloning of the active center of telomerase is a major milestone that sets the stage for more fully understanding the molecular genetics of aging and cancer," said Nobel Laureate Dr. Thomas Cech, a professor at the university.
Telomerase is activated in the late stages of cancer and causes the cells to divide indefinitely. That infinite replication is a major contributor to cancer being a killer.
"Telomerase can be found in every cancer that has been studied," said Ronald Eastman, chief executive of Geron. "This has therapeutic potential in perhaps all cancers."
"Telomerase is very specific to cancer cells. A cancer therapy typically has severe side effects because not only are you killing cancer cells but you are killing normal cells as a result," he said.
David Stone, a biotech analyst at Cowen & Co., warned that the breakthrough should not be welcomed as the "magic bullet" to end cancer.

Stone said that blocking telomerase may prove a flawed therapy. He contends that while a telomerase inhibitor would stop the cancer cell dividing infinitely and convert it into a normal cell, it would not stop it growing and the patient would have to wait for the cell to die of old age.

"The issue is that no one knows at this point whether inhibiting this enzyme in a cancer cell would actually have a big impact on the clinical course of cancer," Stone said. "If a cancer has to die of old age there is some question about how large the tumor will be by the time that happens."
The usefulness of Geron's therapy would depend on whether it could kill the cancer cells rapidly enough to be clinically useful and save the patient.

Stone said a telomerase inhibitor may be most useful as a way of stopping cancer from returning after traditional treatments, such as chemotherapy and surgery, have rid the patient of the bulk of the cancer.
Geron plans to develop a drug treatment ready for clinical trials within one to three years. The drug would then need to be reviewed by regulators, a process that could take many more years.
